70:1.en: A questioner questioned concerning the doom about to fall

70:2.en: Upon the disbelievers, which none can repel

70:3.en: From Allah, Lord of the Ascending Stairways

70:4.ar: تَعۡرُجُ ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ وَٱلرُّوحُ إِلَيۡهِ فِي يَوۡمࣲ كَانَ مِقۡدَارُهُۥ خَمۡسِينَ أَلۡفَ سَنَةࣲ‏
70:4.en: (Whereby) the angels and the Spirit ascend unto Him in a Day whereof the span is fifty thousand years

70:5.en: But be patient (O Muhammad) with a patience fair to see

70:6.en: Lo! they behold it afar off

70:8.en: The day when the sky will become as molten copper

70:9.en: And the hills become as flakes of wool

70:10.en: And no familiar friend will ask a question of his friend

70:11.ar: يُبَصَّرُونَهُمۡۚ يَوَدُّ ٱلۡمُجۡرِمُ لَوۡ يَفۡتَدِي مِنۡ عَذَابِ يَوۡمِئِذِۭ بِبَنِيهِ
70:11.en: Though they will be given sight of them. The guilty man will long to be able to ransom himself from the punishment of that day at the price of his children

70:12.en: And his spouse and his brother

70:13.en: And his kin that harboured him

70:14.ar: وَمَن فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ جَمِيعࣰ ا ثُمَّ يُنجِيهِ
70:14.en: And all that are in the earth, if then it might deliver him

70:15.en: But nay! for lo! it is the fire of hell

70:17.en: It calleth him who turned and fled (from truth)

12:18.ar: وَجَآءُو عَلَىٰ قَمِيصِهِۦ بِدَمࣲ كَذِبࣲۚ قَالَ بَلۡ سَوَّلَتۡ لَكُمۡ أَنفُسُكُمۡ أَمۡرࣰ اۖ فَصَبۡرࣱ جَمِيلࣱۖ وَٱللَّهُ ٱلۡمُسۡتَعَانُ عَلَىٰ مَا تَصِفُونَ
12:18.en: And they came with false blood on his shirt. He said: Nay, but your minds have beguiled you into something. (My course is) comely patience. And Allah it is Whose help is to be sought in that (predicament) which ye describe

73:10.ar: وَٱصۡبِرۡ عَلَىٰ مَا يَقُولُونَ وَٱهۡجُرۡهُمۡ هَجۡرࣰ ا جَمِيلࣰ ا
73:10.en: And bear with patience what they utter, and part from them with a fair leave-taking

39:10.ar: قُلۡ يَٰعِبَادِ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱتَّقُواْ رَبَّكُمۡۚ لِلَّذِينَ أَحۡسَنُواْ فِي هَٰذِهِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا حَسَنَةࣱۗ وَأَرۡضُ ٱللَّهِ وَٰسِعَةٌۗ إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى ٱلصَّٰبِرُونَ أَجۡرَهُم بِغَيۡرِ حِسَابࣲ‏
39:10.en: Say: O My bondmen who believe! Observe your duty to your Lord. For those who do good in this world there is good, and Allah's earth is spacious. Verily the steadfast will be paid their wages without stint

43:67.ar: ٱلۡأَخِلَّآءُ يَوۡمَئِذِۭ بَعۡضُهُمۡ لِبَعۡضٍ عَدُوٌّ إِلَّا ٱلۡمُتَّقِينَ
43:67.en: Friends on that day will be foes one to another, save those who kept their duty (to Allah)

69:19.ar: فَأَمَّا مَنۡ أُوتِيَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِيَمِينِهِۦ فَيَقُولُ هَآؤُمُ ٱقۡرَءُواْ كِتَٰبِيَهۡ
69:19.en: Then, as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: Take, read my book

69:20.en: Surely I knew that I should have to meet my reckoning

69:21.en: Then he will be in blissful state

69:23.en: Whereof the clusters are in easy reach

69:24.ar: كُلُواْ وَٱشۡرَبُواْ هَنِيٓـَٔۢا بِمَآ أَسۡلَفۡتُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأَيَّامِ ٱلۡخَالِيَةِ
69:24.en: (And it will be said unto those therein): Eat and drink at ease for that which ye sent on before you in past days

69:25.ar: وَأَمَّا مَنۡ أُوتِيَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِشِمَالِهِۦ فَيَقُولُ يَٰلَيۡتَنِي لَمۡ أُوتَ كِتَٰبِيَهۡ
69:25.en: But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: Oh, would that I had not been given my book

hsQWzDWkpf4.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Ma'arij, Part 1: Verses 1-18
hsQWzDWkpf4.one_line: Al-Ma'arij opens the practical part of Juz Tabarak: many paths of ascent to Allah, beautiful patience, the gamble of thinking the Day is far, and its horrors.
hsQWzDWkpf4.summary: He places Al-Ma'arij in Juz Tabarak's scheme: after surahs on knowledge, ethics and spiritual reflection, this one turns to behaviour and practice. Allah is Lord of the ascending ways, which he reads as many paths to Him: once the basics are in place, each person finds a niche of good, and Allah is not hard to please. The first command in the juz comes at verse five, beautiful patience. Practical faith has only two states, patience in hardship and gratitude in ease, and the beautiful kind persevers with acceptance rather than quiet resentment, as Yaqub showed. The disbelievers see the Day as far off, a lie the self tells. He likens it to a gambler betting everything, this life and eternity, on the high odds of waking up tomorrow, and warns that time fools everyone. The scenes of melting sky, flying mountains and friends who will not ask about one another follow, with his exam analogy and the exception of friends bound by taqwa, who intercede for each other. The criminal would ransom his children, wife, brother, clan and all humanity, and the flame summons those who turned away and hoarded wealth.

outline.heading: Four domains of Juz Tabarak: knowledge, ethics, spirituality, behaviour
outline.gist: Al-Ma'arij is the fourth surah of the cluster in an entirely Makki juz. Al-Mulk set the requirements of knowledge, Al-Qalam of ethics, Al-Haqqah of spiritual reflection; Al-Ma'arij turns them into behaviour and practice.

outline.heading: The rest of the juz: case studies in dawah
outline.gist: With the four domains in place you become an ambassador of Islam. The remaining surahs show dawah done perfectly without result, dawah done unintentionally with a good result, how to protect yourself, and dawah driven by intellect, fear and desire. All are early Makki surahs.

outline.heading: Recitation of the opening verses
outline.gist: He recites the passage from the questioner's question to the friend who will not ask about his friend.

outline.heading: A questioner asks about the coming punishment
outline.gist: The opening is a device to draw interest: someone asked about the punishment of the Day of Judgment, and for the disbelievers nothing can repel it.

outline.heading: Ma'arij: curved paths of ascent
outline.gist: The word comes from limping, walking off a straight line. Paths that rise into the sky curve, as everything in the cosmos does, so ma'arij are winding ways of ascent.

outline.heading: Many paths to Allah: find your niche
outline.gist: Beyond the shared basics of belief, people ascend through different acts: knowledge, Quran, wealth, striving. The surah's list of behaviours lets everyone find the good they are suited to.

outline.heading: Angels and the spirit ascend in a day of fifty thousand years
outline.gist: He reads the ruh as the collective spirit Allah placed in all people, everything rising to Him when all ends, on a day estimated at fifty thousand years.

outline.heading: No command in Al-Haqqah, the first command here
outline.gist: Al-Haqqah, a surah of spiritual reflection, gives no command at all; this surah of practice gives one in its fifth verse. Such details matter in reading the Quran.

outline.heading: Practical faith has two states: patience or gratitude
outline.gist: Patience is half of faith. In behaviour, faith shows only as perseverance in hardship or gratitude in ease, with no neutral third state; most people find more reasons for gratitude.

outline.heading: Beautiful patience: Yaqub and the wolf story
outline.gist: Allah attaches 'beautiful' to several commanded behaviours. Yaqub knew his sons were lying about the wolf, as parents usually know, and answered with beautiful patience.

outline.heading: Perseverance with acceptance, not resentment
outline.gist: You can persevere while disgruntled. Sabr jamil is perseverance filled with satisfaction in Allah's decree, without anger, disappointment or questioning Him.

outline.heading: Patience as an attitude, rewarded without reckoning
outline.gist: The first practice of the surah is sabr held as a standing attitude. Only the patient are promised reward without account, because hardship is where faith is most vulnerable.

outline.heading: Climbing a mountain in a storm: sabr versus hilm
outline.gist: Sabr is holding on while climbing through rock, wind and rain; hilm is not reacting with anger. Allah is al-Halim, and he contests calling Him as-Sabur since sabr implies difficulty.

outline.heading: Disgruntlement endangers faith; the most tested are the prophets
outline.gist: Objecting to Allah's decree can end in losing faith. The one with sabr expects tests as the story of life, and the higher the rank the greater the test.

outline.heading: They see it far: the lie the self tells
outline.gist: The nafs builds a narrative that death and reckoning are far off, so nothing needs to change today. Even if life is long, the Hour comes suddenly, when Allah chooses.

outline.heading: Without certainty you are playing probabilities
outline.gist: Probability is dangerous when much is at stake. Gamblers who bet everything because the odds look good are bound to lose, and some lose everything.

outline.heading: Gambling eternity on good odds
outline.gist: Everyone plays the disbelievers' gamble: ninety-nine per cent sure of waking tomorrow, staking this life and eternity on it. No poker player would make such a bet.

outline.heading: How the odds fool you: the gambler's early wins
outline.gist: Every safe night makes you more confident, the way betting companies let new players win before the real odds take everything. The self does the same with the belief that death is far.

outline.heading: The truthful stance: change now
outline.gist: With a guarantee of life he would wait and run a boot camp before the end, but there is none. A real possibility of dying soon demands change now, not after graduation, marriage or a job.

outline.heading: Why a surah on practice opens this way
outline.gist: Behaviour will not change until this piece is settled. He ties the opening together: the One with countless paths to please Him, the day of fifty thousand years, beautiful patience now.

outline.heading: We see it near: how time fools us
outline.gist: Ask anyone of seventy or eighty and they feel it passed in a moment. A hundred years means nothing in hindsight; whatever ends is near, and only the endless is far.

outline.heading: Molten sky and mountains like carded wool
outline.gist: The fabric of the universe melts like molten metal, and the mountains, so sturdy and magnificent, fly apart like teased-out wool.

outline.heading: The intimate friend will not ask about his friend
outline.gist: Terror makes even the closest friend silent. The ultimate selfishness takes over as home and safety vanish, and each knows the day is about his own account.

outline.heading: No one knows you but you
outline.gist: Everyone wears a front; only Allah and you know you. Without self-awareness you will be introduced to yourself on the Day, a bad time to meet yourself.

outline.heading: The unprepared after an exam
outline.gist: Students who did not prepare avoid their friends before and after the exam, a small picture of the Day for those who did not prepare.

outline.heading: Friends bound by taqwa: the scholars' covenant
outline.gist: Close friends become enemies except the God-conscious. Scholars take a covenant with students that neither enters Paradise without asking about the other; he holds such covenants with many.

outline.heading: The pious intercede for their people
outline.gist: Those close to Allah have the standing to plead for family and friends; sometimes the intercession is accepted and sometimes not.

outline.heading: Recitation of the next passage: yawmi'idhin with a kasra
outline.gist: The snapshot of the unprepared continues. In verse 11 yawmi'idhin is read with a kasra on the mim, one of two places in the Quran, so take care when reciting.

outline.heading: Made to see one another
outline.gist: Allah makes loved ones see each other, so the silence is not forgetfulness, like two people pretending not to have noticed each other. The one given his book in his right hand, by contrast, calls others to read it.

outline.heading: The mujrim: one who broke Allah's laws
outline.gist: The criminal here is not someone who broke a random civil law but one who broke the laws Allah set for what may and may not be done.

outline.heading: The ransom: children, wife, brother, clan, everyone
outline.gist: He would ransom himself with his children, wife, brother, his fasilah, the social network that took him in, and all humanity.

outline.heading: What did he see?
outline.gist: Picture his face as he offers to burn everyone he spent his life protecting. Ask what horror is reflected in his eyes that makes him say it.

outline.heading: Laza: the flame that tears at the scalp
outline.gist: No, that is not how it works: it is a raging flame that strips away the front of the head, the part with which a person presents himself.

outline.heading: It calls those who turned away
outline.gist: The fire summons those who turned their backs on the paths of ascent. Allah is not hard to please: the basics, then one good you are suited to.

outline.heading: Those who gathered and hoarded
outline.gist: A picture of the self-centred who trust a bank balance for security. Earning wealth is not haram; holding it back without paying its due is.

themes.note: Sabr jamil is the surah's first command: perseverance held as a lasting attitude, filled with acceptance rather than resentment, rewarded without reckoning.

themes.label: Mortality, death and preparing for it
themes.note: Believing death and reckoning are far off is a gamble with eternity; uncertainty alone demands change now, and time fools everyone.

themes.label: The Hereafter: resurrection, judgment, paradise, hellfire

themes.label: Brotherhood, companionship and friendship

themes.label: Wealth, asceticism (zuhd), consumerism and money
themes.note: The flame calls those who gathered and withheld wealth, trusting a bank balance for security; earning is not the sin, withholding the due is.

oQSC8jL67iM.speaker: adnan
oQSC8jL67iM.speaker_note: gives his yearly fiqh of Ramadan class at his masjid; refers to timing his imams and leading tarawih for over 25 years
oQSC8jL67iM.title: The Fiqh of Ramadan (2025)
oQSC8jL67iM.one_line: His yearly class on the rulings of fasting: intention, invalidators, disputed medical cases, exemptions, expiations, sunnahs, tarawih, zakat al-fitr, Eid, and a long Q&A.
oQSC8jL67iM.summary: He opens by insisting that the mechanical and spiritual sides of worship are equally important; favouring either leaves a Muslim unbalanced for life, and this class covers the mechanics. Intention must exist before Fajr, though he follows Imam Malik's single intention for the month. His master rule is that intentional intake of anything medically nourishing breaks the fast; from it he lists six invalidators, noting that IV nourishment and smoking break the fast even unintentionally, and six agreed non-invalidators. On disputed cases he accepts inhalers and drops that do not reach the throat, but holds that any IV and any suppository breaks the fast, while dismissing the yearly bidet question. Illness can turn from a permission into a command not to fast, because health outranks perfecting worship. He explains travel, pregnancy, breastfeeding and severe fatigue, making up days before the next Ramadan, and the major and minor expiations, advising caution where scholars differ. He covers the sunnahs of iftar and suhoor, fasting from sin, tarawih judged by time and Quran rather than rakah count, and zakat al-fitr, insisting that zakat stay local until the community's own poor are cared for. He argues a city needs a few large Eid prayers, not dozens, and answers many practical questions on medications, blood tests, dental work and travel.

outline.heading: Majority opinions, and following your local imam
outline.gist: He gives a broad picture of majority positions and flags disputes; those praying with him can simply follow his choices, as anyone can follow the imam of the masjid they attend.

outline.heading: Ramadan as the high season of spirituality
outline.gist: The early generations prepared for months and asked for acceptance for months afterwards; he has rarely seen real change in a person or community outside Ramadan.

outline.heading: Mechanical and spiritual are equally important
outline.gist: Every act of worship has an outward form and an inner meaning; ranking one above the other leaves a Muslim unbalanced for life. This session covers the form, the next the spirit.

outline.heading: Intention must come before Fajr
outline.gist: Intention is a condition for fasting and simply means knowing you fast tomorrow; waking for suhoor shows it. He follows Imam Malik's single intention for the month, while voluntary fasts can be intended late in the morning.

outline.heading: The general rule: intentional nourishment
outline.gist: Anything taken in intentionally that gives the body any degree of medical nourishment breaks the fast; the classical rulings rest on this rule, and medicine now defines nourishment more precisely.

outline.heading: Invalidator: eating and drinking on purpose
outline.gist: The obvious one, and only when intentional.

outline.heading: Invalidator: intercourse or its equivalent
outline.gist: Intercourse or deliberately reaching orgasm breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Invalidator: deliberate vomiting
outline.gist: The first three only break the fast when intentional.

outline.heading: Invalidator: parenteral nourishment, even unintentional
outline.gist: Nutrition bags, saline or Ringer's lactate entering the bloodstream break the fast whether or not the person intended it.

outline.heading: Invalidator: smoking, even forgetfully
outline.gist: Any smoking or vaping breaks the fast even if done absent-mindedly, because the forgiveness for forgetful eating is a text about pure worship that cannot be extended by analogy.

outline.heading: Invalidator: menstruation and postpartum bleeding
outline.gist: These end the fast immediately; he recaps the six invalidators.

outline.heading: Does not break: brushing and miswak
outline.gist: Brushing and miswak are fine at any time of day, but toothpaste swallowed by mistake does break the fast, so brushing carries a risk.

outline.heading: Does not break: eating forgetfully
outline.gist: Let a forgetful eater finish rather than panicking them into swallowing; you are not the fasting police. Fasting is between a person and Allah, unlike the childhood tongue-colour checks adults once used on him.

outline.heading: Does not break: a wet dream
outline.gist: Unintended pleasure during sleep, by day or night, does not affect the fast.

outline.heading: Does not break: non-nourishing injections
outline.gist: Based on modern collective fatwas, intramuscular or subcutaneous blood thinners, antibiotics and insulin do not break the fast.

outline.heading: Does not break: swallowing saliva
outline.gist: Even deliberately collected saliva does not break the fast, though it is disliked.

outline.heading: Does not break: the unavoidable after wudu
outline.gist: Make wudu normally; traces that slip down are unavoidable and forgiven, but deliberately leaving water hoping it goes down is negligence you are liable for.

outline.heading: Disputed: inhalers
outline.gist: Scholars split roughly evenly; he holds that inhalers needed for asthma or COPD do not break the fast because they only open the airways and give no nourishment, unlike smoking.

outline.heading: Disputed: eye and ear drops
outline.gist: Prescribed drops do not break the fast in his view, but if a drop trickles down the throat the fast is broken by agreement.

outline.heading: Disputed: non-nourishing IV infusions
outline.gist: Fluid filling the veins reverses the dehydration that is part of fasting, so he holds any IV, even antibiotics or contrast for a scan, breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Using a bidet does not break the fast
outline.gist: He calls the yearly question absurd: washing with water was always part of Islamic practice and no one drinks from the other end.

outline.heading: Disputed: suppositories
outline.gist: The classical texts mention insertion breaking the fast and adults rarely need suppositories while healthy enough to fast, so he holds they break it.

outline.heading: Illness: from permission to command
outline.gist: When a physician says fasting will harm you, breaking the fast becomes obligatory, because bodily health outranks perfecting worship; ordinary illness only requires making up the days.

outline.heading: The elderly woman on dialysis
outline.gist: Every year an elderly woman whose family and doctor forbid fasting calls hoping for permission, and hangs up when he tells her she is not allowed to fast.

outline.heading: Travel: stricter than for prayer
outline.gist: Breaking the fast needs travel beyond about 80 km; while moving you may break it daily, but longer stays in one place range from three or four days to fifteen, so ask an imam.

outline.heading: Comfortable travel is still travel, but be wise
outline.gist: The permission holds even in first class, but he advises fasting when possible since missed days are hard to make up; the Prophet discouraged fasting on journeys that were then gruelling.

outline.heading: Exemption: pregnancy and breastfeeding
outline.gist: Both are valid reasons, with the expiation question covered later.

outline.heading: Exemption: severe fatigue
outline.gist: A roofer in summer must intend to fast every night and break only when he fears for his safety, even every day; a breadwinner is not required to stop working for the month.

outline.heading: Fatigue owes only the make-up day
outline.gist: Breaking the fast from severe fatigue carries no expiation; the days are made up in short winter days.

outline.heading: Make up days before the next Ramadan
outline.gist: Spread make-up days across the year rather than cramming them before Ramadan; missing the deadline needs repentance and one payment per day, owed once only.

outline.heading: Unknown or decades of missed days
outline.gist: Estimate the highest likely number and add a margin; someone who repents after years of not fasting at all should pay for those days and start fasting, as if newly Muslim.

outline.heading: Major expiation: intercourse in a Ramadan day
outline.gist: All schools agree it is owed, by both spouses if both consented: sixty consecutive days of fasting or feeding sixty people, about $1,200. He met someone who fasted all sixty days and saw great blessing in it.

outline.heading: Deliberate eating: the day may be lost forever
outline.gist: Scholars differ on a major expiation for eating out of anger; he holds only the make-up day is owed, while noting some scholars say such a day can never be made up at all.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: the terminally ill
outline.gist: Those with incurable conditions pay about $20 a day; some scholars allow paying the month up front, others day by day, since a person who dies mid-month owes only the days passed.

outline.heading: Those exempt still honour the fast
outline.gist: Eat only what is needed, out of public view, and join the family at iftar; this is the Prophet's teaching, and a physician should confirm whether a condition is curable.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: the elderly
outline.gist: He suggests anyone over 75 qualifies; older bodies have less reserve and fasting must never tip someone into dependency.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: postponing make-up days
outline.gist: Owed once for each day carried past the next Ramadan.

outline.heading: Minor expiation: pregnancy and breastfeeding
outline.gist: Abu Hanifa does not require it and others tie it to whether the fast was broken for the baby's sake; to stay safe, he tells husbands to pay it.

outline.heading: Where expiations should be paid
outline.gist: Asked whether expiations can go abroad, he says they are preferred locally and defers the full answer to his discussion of zakat.

outline.heading: Late suhoor, early iftar
outline.gist: These two sunnahs protect the sharia from people adding fasting time out of misplaced piety; Allah wants exactly the time He set.

outline.heading: Break the fast on dates or water
outline.gist: Fresh dates, then dried, then water; someone who dislikes dates should still break on water rather than ordinary food.

outline.heading: Dua at iftar, and when to pray Maghrib
outline.gist: Make dua before or after breaking the fast. Breaking on dates and water, praying promptly and then eating lets you eat better and unrushed, though both orders are allowed.

outline.heading: Fast from sin
outline.gist: Abstaining from halal food, drink and spouse while committing haram makes no sense; Allah has no need of the fast of one who lives by falsehood.

outline.heading: The Syrian muezzin's glass of water
outline.gist: In Syria someone handed the muezzin water after the first takbir so he could break his fast on time and then finish the adhan, a custom he loves.

outline.heading: Tarawih: numbers never mattered
outline.gist: The Prophet prayed eight, ten or thirteen and Imam Malik counted more to match Makkah's extra rounds; what matters is time, presence of heart and closeness to Allah.

outline.heading: Hear the whole Quran and stay to the end
outline.gist: Choose a masjid that completes the Quran at least once, as earlier generations did two or three times, and stay with the imam to earn the reward of a full night.

outline.heading: Why he times every imam to the minute
outline.gist: After over 25 years of timing every format, he holds imams to the minute and trains their pace and sound, out of respect for people trying to pray the whole night.

outline.heading: Eat lightly before tarawih
outline.gist: Overeating turns tarawih into exhausted yoga; since 1998 he breaks his fast on dates, water and soup and eats one meal after tarawih. Home and masjid are both valid, but the masjid is better.

outline.heading: Zakat al-fitr: when to give it
outline.gist: Opinions range from the first day of Ramadan, the Shafi'i mid-month, to the majority's few days before Eid; mid-Ramadan gives charities time to deliver, and after the Eid prayer it is too late for most scholars.

outline.heading: Zakat al-fitr: amount and who pays
outline.gist: About $20 to $25 a person; the breadwinner pays for himself, his wife, children and a fetus past 120 days.

outline.heading: Zakat must stay local first
outline.gist: Sending a 40,000-strong community's zakat abroad while local families go hungry is a collective sin; in 2018 he was shown single mothers in the city with nothing to feed their children. Give abroad, to Gaza, Sudan and elsewhere, once local need is met.

outline.heading: Eid prayer: a few large gatherings
outline.gist: Eid is a near-obligatory congregational prayer in an open space; thirty-five Eid prayers in one city defeats its purpose, and three large venues would serve everyone.

outline.heading: Eid reaches Muslims who never come
outline.gist: Most of his lessons preach to the choir; Eid gathers thousands who never attend, so it is where outreach and connection should happen. Timing is flexible.

outline.heading: Women attend Eid even while menstruating
outline.gist: Unlike other prayers, women are recommended to attend Eid with their families whatever their state.

outline.heading: Never an Eid prayer in this building
outline.gist: Eid belongs outdoors, and cramming a thousand people into the masjid would make them miserable; he would rather pray in the snow.

outline.heading: Q&A: eye drops reaching the throat
outline.gist: Drops are fine unless they go down the throat, in which case the fast is lost.

outline.heading: Q&A: who owes zakat al-fitr
outline.gist: Every free Muslim adult with enough for the day owes it, students included, unless a parent pays for them; his own father still insists on paying his.

outline.heading: Cash or food: a settled difference
outline.gist: The yearly online war over cash payment revives a debate settled a millennium ago; the Hanafis and others allow cash, charities buy food with it, and no one should call names over it.

outline.heading: Q&A: giving zakat al-fitr through a charity
outline.gist: Delegating to a trusted charity fulfils the duty; charities pay out mid-Ramadan and use late donations to cover what they already gave, but giving at the last minute is still wrong.

outline.heading: Q&A: IV treatment, temporary or chronic
outline.gist: A needed IV still breaks the fast; temporary treatment means making up the days, while daily lifelong treatment such as dialysis means paying the minor expiation.

outline.heading: Q&A: profanity does not break the fast
outline.gist: No word invalidates the fast, but sinful speech, sight or conduct costs its reward and acceptance.

outline.heading: Q&A: time-release pills and vitamins
outline.gist: Anything by mouth during the day breaks the fast; a prescribed long-acting pill taken at night is fine unless taken to make fasting easier. Vitamins are not nourishment.

outline.heading: Q&A: blood donation versus blood tests
outline.gist: Narrations on cupping differ, so to be safe he holds that donating blood or hijama breaks the fast, while small blood tests are like a cut and do not.

outline.heading: Q&A: nicotine patches
outline.gist: Case by case, but following the fatwa of North American scholars he advises wearing the patch overnight and removing it by day.

outline.heading: Q&A: mouthwash and iron infusions
outline.gist: Mouthwash is fine if not swallowed; an iron infusion is fluid in the vein and breaks the fast.

outline.heading: Q&A: tasting food while cooking
outline.gist: Cooks and chefs may touch food to the tip of the tongue, but must spit out the saliva it produces.

outline.heading: Q&A: anemia
outline.gist: Chronic anemia diagnosed as preventing fasting means paying expiation; a temporary condition means making up the days.

outline.heading: Q&A: fatigue is your own judgment
outline.gist: You may break the fast when you fear for your physical or psychological wellbeing, but no imam can decide that for you over the phone.

outline.heading: Q&A: drivers, and travel only to break the fast
outline.gist: Truck and bus drivers who are always travelling may pay expiation like the chronically ill, but driving 80 km just to eat a burger, or travelling for sin, earns no permission.

outline.heading: Q&A: dental cleaning and extractions
outline.gist: Swallowed water or blood breaks the fast, but a needed procedure is a valid reason; local anaesthetic is not nourishment, and the day is simply made up.

cCvrxqrlw30.title: Surat Al-Haqqah Part 5: Verses 36-52
cCvrxqrlw30.one_line: Aligning passion with intellect so you come to want what is right, Umar's path to Islam through these verses, and the warning against fabricating revelation.
cCvrxqrlw30.summary: He argues that the spiritual dimension of faith is neglected because people are uncomfortable with emotion and materialism reduces feelings to chemistry. When the heart wants haram while the mind follows Allah, life becomes a painful dissonance; but the nafs, a primitive yet devoted servant, can be trained like a child until passion aligns with belief. Yusuf refusing temptation at seventeen shows a believer can come to find haram repugnant, and the hadith on desires following the Prophet's teaching defines complete faith. Melodious recitation, nasheed and companions like 'Abbad ibn Bishr, who kept praying with arrows in him, show worship enjoyed rather than endured. Feelings cannot be switched off directly but change indirectly through thoughts, company, exposure and reflection. In the closing verses Allah swears by what is seen and unseen that this is the word of a noble messenger, not a poet or soothsayer. He tells how Umar, an all-or-nothing man, was moved by a servant girl's steadfastness and then by hearing these verses at the Ka'bah answer his own thoughts. The warning that even the Prophet would have been destroyed for inventing a word is for us, against attributing to Allah what He did not say. The Quran is a reminder, a regret for deniers and certain truth, and the surah's only command is to glorify Allah.

outline.heading: The neglected spiritual dimension
outline.gist: Muslims prioritise knowledge and then ethics, while emotional and spiritual reflection is neglected because many feel awkward with it.

outline.heading: Materialism and the double-edged sword of emotion
outline.gist: Modern science often reduces emotion to chemistry; preachers who exploit emotion sell illusions, but the Quran treats it methodically.

outline.heading: When passion and intellect pull apart
outline.gist: A Muslim follows truth wherever it is, so facts should not cause dissonance; the real pain is a heart that wants haram while the mind follows Allah.

outline.heading: You can come to want what is right
outline.gist: With emotional reflection the carrot can be moved in line with the goal, so the powerful nafs pulls you forward.

outline.heading: Loving the work you do
outline.gist: People who love their jobs, like a scientist absorbed in research, are happiest because desire and duty align.

outline.heading: Taming the nafs like a child
outline.gist: The nafs wants food, sex, status and attention and is your biggest fan but ignorant; trained over time, as children learn to love reading, it changes.

outline.heading: The grass always greener
outline.gist: Men tend to look outside their marriages; the question is whether one can come to despise what is haram rather than forever longing for it.

outline.heading: Yusuf at seventeen
outline.gist: Young, enslaved, unknown and pursued in private, he refused because disgust at haram outweighed desire; complete faith is desire following the Prophet's teaching.

outline.heading: Nasheed to move the heart
outline.gist: Let your passion be invested in love of Allah, the Quran and the Prophet; nasheed arose to stir hearts already convinced intellectually.

outline.heading: Why the Quran is recited melodiously
outline.gist: No other serious book is sung; the art exists so hearts are moved, which is why congregations care about an imam's voice.

outline.heading: We all seek what moves us
outline.gist: Favourite reciters, speakers, Ramadan and sacred places show everyone thirsts for spiritual stimulus; the early Muslims loved worship.

outline.heading: 'Abbad ibn Bishr keeps praying with arrows in him
outline.gist: On guard duty he pulled out two arrows and continued because he would not cut short his surah; such reports are too many to dismiss.

outline.heading: Old struggles become jokes
outline.gist: When passion aligns with belief, the struggle moves to guarding sincerity; this explains the Prophet's transformation of Arabia in 23 years.

outline.heading: Seek people who have all three
outline.gist: Some are passionate but untaught; when you find someone with knowledge, practice and love together, stay near them.

outline.heading: Recap of the surah's emotional journey
outline.gist: From the nations to the Day and the two books; the man in the left hand neither revered Allah nor fed the poor.

outline.heading: Neither religious nor decent
outline.gist: He found goodness neither through faith nor on his own, so he has no hamim, and Allah erases him from the memories of those who loved him.

outline.heading: Food only from ghislin
outline.gist: The khati'un are those who knowingly persist in wrong, unlike people who err and repent.

outline.heading: Feelings change but not by switch
outline.gist: Couples who once adored each other fight in court; you control actions and beliefs directly but feelings only indirectly.

outline.heading: I don't want to want it
outline.gist: That wish is the first step; thoughts, company, exposure and reflection gradually change what you love and fade low desires.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet bore so much abuse
outline.gist: Having tasted such joy, he wanted it for everyone, even those trying to kill him.

outline.heading: Learning that makes people rigid
outline.gist: Some grow harsher as they learn fiqh and theology because their hearts are not invested.

outline.heading: I need not swear, yet I swear
outline.gist: La uqsimu says this is too factual to need an oath, since excessive oaths backfire, yet Allah swears to emphasise it.

outline.heading: By what you see and what you do not
outline.gist: The tangible and the unmeasurable, like faith and feelings, which no scan can show.

outline.heading: The word of a noble messenger; Umar's all-in nature
outline.gist: Umar only moved when heart and mind agreed, and committed fully to whatever he believed.

outline.heading: Umar before Islam
outline.gist: Fully invested in Quraysh's order, he harmed Muslims, later laughing and making amends; once Muslim he changed Mecca in a day.

outline.heading: Umar and the servant girl's steadfastness
outline.gist: The more he tormented a young Muslim servant, the firmer she grew, making him first wonder what lay behind this faith.

outline.heading: Umar circling the Ka'bah
outline.gist: Finding the assembly closed, he did tawaf and slowed near the Prophet to hear his recitation of Al-Haqqah.

outline.heading: Verses answering Umar's thoughts
outline.gist: He thought a poet and the verse said not a poet; he thought a soothsayer and it said not a soothsayer; then revelation from the Lord of the worlds.

outline.heading: Umar's sister and the meaning of the verses
outline.gist: He later set out to kill the Prophet and was redirected to his Muslim sister; he struggled because he assumed it was fabricated, and these verses alone are enough to reflect on.

outline.heading: Had he fabricated anything
outline.gist: Taqawwul is attributing to someone what they did not say; the verse addresses the Prophet, who never did so.

outline.heading: Seized by the right hand; the aorta severed
outline.gist: Al-yamin conveys strength or seizing by the right arm; al-watin is most likely the aorta, and no one could shield him.

outline.heading: Not even the most beloved would be spared
outline.gist: If Allah's most beloved would be destroyed for one invented word, how much more anyone else; Allah also warned him he nearly inclined to them.

outline.heading: Would a fabricator include this?
outline.gist: No impostor in weak early Mecca would recite such a warning about himself; it is for us, never to attribute to Allah what He did not say or mean.

outline.heading: A reminder for the mindful
outline.gist: The Quran and Sunnah together keep rekindling the heart's fire, which dies if unattended.

outline.heading: Deniers and regret
outline.gist: Some will deny regardless of evidence; everyone will wish they had reflected more, but the deepest regret belongs to those who refused.

outline.heading: Certain truth and the one command
outline.gist: Haqq al-yaqin is truth wrapped in certainty; after a surah with no commands, the only instruction is to glorify the name of your Lord.

-JX0AC40gVY.summary: Continuing a session on the fiqh of fasting, he separates the major expiation, owed by consensus only for intercourse, from the minor one of feeding a poor person per day, and adopts the easier view that deliberate eating requires only making up the day. Five cases owe the minor expiation: chronic illness, old age, delaying make-up past the next Ramadan, and pregnancy or nursing, where after laying out Hanafi and Shafi'i reasoning he advises paying in every case to avoid disagreement. Temporary illness, travel and exhaustion require only make-up. He presents delaying suhoor and hastening iftar as safeguards against inventing extra worship, describes breaking the fast on dates or water and making dua around iftar, and stresses that lies do not void the fast but void its reward. Eating after fajr by mistake leaves the fast valid; breaking early does not. On taraweeh he insists the number of rak'at never mattered, criticizes rushed prayers, and recommends staying with the imam who completes the Quran. He urges that zakat al-fitr reach local poor Muslims, accepts both cash and food, explains Eid prayer as a single communal gathering, and closes by asking people to follow one masjid's timings and imam for unity.

outline.heading: Minor and major expiation
outline.gist: The major expiation applies by consensus only to intercourse; he takes the easier view that deliberate eating requires make-up only.

outline.heading: Chronic illness: fidyah instead of fasting
outline.gist: One with incurable illness does not intend to fast, pays a poor person's meal per day, may pay in advance, and heirs pay for days passed if he dies mid-month.

outline.heading: Old age
outline.gist: The elderly who tire easily may break the fast and pay fidyah even if healthy.

outline.heading: Delaying make-up past the next Ramadan
outline.gist: Unmade days carried into the next Ramadan owe fidyah once, not again each year.

outline.heading: Pregnancy and nursing
outline.gist: Abu Hanifah requires no fidyah, the others require it when fearing for the child, based on al-Shafi'i's principle of another soul; he advises paying in all cases.

outline.heading: Tasting food while cooking
outline.gist: Touching food to the tip of the tongue and spitting does not break the fast.

outline.heading: Excuses that need only make-up
outline.gist: Temporary illness, travel and severe exhaustion require only making up the days; he restates the five cases that owe fidyah.

outline.heading: Delaying suhoor and hastening iftar guard the religion
outline.gist: These sunnahs block people from adding extra hours of fasting and competing in excess that harms work and study.

outline.heading: Breaking the fast on dates or water
outline.gist: Fresh dates, then dry dates, then water; those who dislike dates follow the sunnah with water.

outline.heading: Dua before and after iftar
outline.gist: Both views have strong evidence; make a short dua before and after, ideally with your family.

outline.heading: Fasting from sins: the fast stays valid but loses its reward
outline.gist: Abstaining from the lawful while committing the unlawful makes no sense; lying voids the reward, not the fast.

outline.heading: Mistakes at dawn and dusk
outline.gist: Drinking after fajr by mistake keeps the fast valid because night is the default; breaking before maghrib requires make-up; a minority view on the adhan is noted.

outline.heading: Taraweeh: the number of rak'at never mattered
outline.gist: The Prophet prayed eight, ten or thirteen, Umar gathered people on twenty, Imam Malik prayed more to match the tawaf of Makkah.

outline.heading: Why taraweeh here has no rest breaks
outline.gist: The surrounding society does not accommodate the fasting person's sleep, so imams must be wise in how they lead.

outline.heading: Rushed prayers defeat the purpose
outline.gist: A prayer reduced to minutes empties its meaning; long standing is best, and a quarter hour of real recitation at home is better than racing through.

outline.heading: Stay with the imam until he finishes
outline.gist: Praying with the imam who completes the Quran until he ends earns the reward of a whole night; the imam means whoever runs the programme.

outline.heading: Zakat al-fitr must reach local poor Muslims
outline.gist: With some 40,000 Muslims in the city, sending all zakat abroad while neighbours are in need is a shared sin.

outline.heading: Cash or food: a valid difference
outline.gist: Both positions have sound evidence; attacking those who pay in cash is ignorance of how the religion works.

outline.heading: Zakat al-fitr to non-Muslims
outline.gist: Permissible under a Muslim polity with a common treasury, but a minority should first care for its own while giving charity to all.

outline.heading: Eid prayer: its status and one gathering
outline.gist: Views range from sunnah to communal or individual obligation; it should be one open-air gathering, not dozens of separate prayers.

outline.heading: Paying zakat al-fitr before the Eid prayer
outline.gist: Some accept it until noon, but pay before Eid to stay clear of disagreement.

outline.heading: Abandoning Eid prayer entirely
outline.gist: A community that refuses Eid prayer altogether must be made to pray it, as it is a symbol of Islam.

outline.heading: Amount and who it is paid for
outline.gist: About $20 per person, including a fetus past 120 days.

outline.heading: Timing of Eid prayer and takbirat
outline.gist: Eid al-Fitr is slightly delayed and Eid al-Adha hastened; every culture's takbir form is acceptable.

outline.heading: Delegating zakat and fixing a yearly zakat date
outline.gist: Appointing an agent to distribute zakat is agreed upon; one can make the first of Ramadan the annual zakat date.

outline.heading: Breaking the fast at the start of the adhan
outline.gist: Break at the first 'Allahu akbar'; in the Levant the muezzin would pause to break his fast.

outline.heading: Differing timetables
outline.gist: Differences between local mosques and apps are acceptable; do not judge the sunset by eye.

outline.heading: Follow one masjid and one imam
outline.gist: A diverse congregation unites by following the local imam in communal worship; keep your own madhhab for private worship, and the imam bears the responsibility.

5fPW9aOz27w.speaker_note: Refers to Damascus as his city and to his own debates defending Islam; continues his Understanding Islam series.
5fPW9aOz27w.title: Understanding Islam: The Outcomes (Part 2)
5fPW9aOz27w.one_line: Islam must be judged by its collective outcomes; it worked once spectacularly, so when it fails today the fault is in our practice, not the theory.
5fPW9aOz27w.summary: Closing his Understanding Islam series, the sheikh argues that every faith and ideology drifts from its purpose unless it builds in checks and balances, the way earlier prophets' teachings were lost. Muslims must periodically ask what Islam is for and judge themselves by its outcomes. After recapping the individual benefits of his three-dimension model, he turns to the collective: if Islam helped individuals but failed the group, it would not be worth holding. He admits he wins every theoretical debate but squirms when asked why Muslim communities are not thriving. His evidence that it once worked is history: on an animated map of empires, green explodes across three continents within thirty years of the Prophet's death, and people converted willingly because they found the compassionate, just community their souls longed for. He cites Ibrahim's prayer and the Prophet's predictions of a society where no one accepts charity and a woman travels alone safely. If those outcomes are missing, either the principles are wrong or we are doing it wrong. In the second khutbah he lists three promised outcomes (reform built on the five objectives of the Shariah, guidance spreading, peace and justice) and warns that Canada's freedoms leave Muslims no excuse.

outline.heading: Faith without the thread
outline.gist: People know certain dos and don'ts and carry cultural baggage, but miss the thread that sews it all together. Any faith or ideology without checks and balances loses sight of what it was designed to do and gets lost in details.

outline.heading: Every faith began with a prophet
outline.gist: Allah sent His prophets with essentially the same teachings, and over time the hand of man corrupted them. Every faith on earth, from Hinduism and Buddhism to the faiths of the Americas, began with a prophet.

outline.heading: Knowledge leaves with the scholars
outline.gist: Having the Quran on the shelf as the Prophet recited it is not enough. Allah does not pull knowledge out of people's chests; it goes when scholars go and no one cares to learn, and the chains of knowledge are lost.

outline.heading: Checks and balances: judge by outcomes
outline.gist: We must periodically ask what Islam is based on and what it should achieve. If you cannot see the foundation, look at the outcomes, as a company reviews its vision, mission and values; this keeps you from getting lost in details best left to specialists.

outline.heading: The model so far
outline.gist: Recap: invest equally in Islam, Iman and Ihsan, keep mortality and accountability pinned on your board, and understand the premise of the journey, giving now to receive later. Individually that brings fulfillment, synchrony, direction and integrity.

outline.heading: Islam must serve the collective
outline.gist: Humans can only exist in groups, so a way of life that does not let the group prosper is not functional. If Islam helped individuals but failed together, he says, throw it out; but this is exactly what Islam did, and the Prophet left an example.

outline.heading: Winning the theory, squirming at the practice
outline.gist: In theory he can mop the floor with any opponent, but when asked why Muslims are not thriving he has to hide behind a pillar. He has strong evidence it worked once, but no convincing answer for why it does not work now, and without a demonstration the case for Islam is weak.

outline.heading: Not a one-man show
outline.gist: Had the Prophet lived to see the empire, Islam could be dismissed as one man's magnificence. Allah willed that he die when Islam was barely in Arabia, much of it held only by treaties.

outline.heading: Green explodes on the map
outline.gist: Run an animated map of the old world: Roman red, Persian black, colours moving back and forth for millennia. Around the seventh century green explodes like a bucket of paint, from a dot in Arabia to three continents in under thirty years.

outline.heading: It grew after he died
outline.gist: There is no other historical example. Thirty years after his death in 11 AH, Islam was the largest empire the world had seen, and far more people accepted it after his death than during his life, because what he taught worked for the group.

outline.heading: From rough desert people to tears at night
outline.gist: He took a rigid, rough, illiterate people who had never been governed, living in an unforgiving climate, and within a decade or two had them standing all night sobbing over the Quran. The community was not perfect, but it worked.

outline.heading: They came to witness it
outline.gist: People travelled from across Arabia, not interested in religion, because they heard that a man of Quraysh was living in the house of a man of Madinah as a brother. It sounded insane, so they came to see it.

outline.heading: Never forced: the minorities of Damascus
outline.gist: In historic neighbourhoods of Damascus, communities of seven or eight hundred people have kept faiths found nowhere else for centuries. No one was forced to accept Islam; the claim exists because people cannot explain the spread any other way.

outline.heading: The spirit yearns for this
outline.gist: The soul yearns for a community built on compassion, selflessness, service, equality and justice, so when the companions brought it, people accepted because they wanted to. That is why most of us are Muslim; the collective functionality has to be brought back, because that is where Islam shines.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's vision
outline.gist: Philosophers' utopias disappoint. The Quran repeats Ibrahim's vision: a land of safety and security whose people have enough, where monotheism is clear and those who stray find a loving hand back to Allah rather than destruction.

outline.heading: The Prophet's vision
outline.gist: A time will come when a man takes out his charity and finds no one to accept it because everyone is doing well, and a woman will travel alone to Makkah for Hajj fearing no one but Allah.

outline.heading: Either the principles or the practice
outline.gist: If you do not get the outcome, either the principles were wrong or you are not doing it right; there is no third option. When neither individuals nor the ummah see the outcomes, we need a revision of how we follow the teachings.

outline.heading: Glad tidings, and deeds done for this world
outline.gist: A narration in Musnad Ahmad gives this ummah glad tidings of ease, status, victory and strength on earth, and warns that whoever does a deed of the hereafter for worldly gain gets nothing. Follow the rules correctly and the dunya will be taken care of.

outline.heading: Outcome 1: reform
outline.gist: Like Shu'ayb, who wanted only reform as far as he was able, societies gain social, financial and ethical reform: they can see what is wrong and fix it, and good is clearly defined and encouraged.

outline.heading: The five objectives of the Shariah
outline.gist: Islam exists to preserve five things: freedom of belief, life, wealth, intellect and dignity, so that people can think freely and walk with their heads high. That is how a society is reformed.

outline.heading: Outcome 2: guidance spreading
outline.gist: Allah defines victory not by swords but by people entering His religion in crowds. We do not want to remain a minority; we want others to take the guidance further than we did and share in the reward.

outline.heading: Outcome 3: peace and justice for everyone
outline.gist: Equality, equity, fairness, justice and peace spread to everyone, not just Muslims. It already worked once, in a transformation unparalleled before or since.

outline.heading: The problem is the practice
outline.gist: The theory is not the problem, and he will win that argument. Turning it into practice is much harder than he thought when he was young and idealistic.

outline.heading: Prove it to Allah
outline.gist: Go back to the fundamentals and build up as individuals and communities. To be with Muhammad and his companions, we must show we can do with what he left something like what they did; failing scares him.

outline.heading: Freedoms others never had
outline.gist: Here no one writes your name down for praying Fajr, attending a late dars, learning Quran or starting a charity. Either you never lived without these freedoms or you forgot, and either way you are at fault for missing the opportunity.

outline.heading: What will we tell Allah?
outline.gist: Our surroundings carry poor values, but we still have the chance to prove Islam works. He would rather live without freedom than explain why we lacked empathy, brotherhood and unity and neglected our youth and vulnerable. Were we coerced? Who are we blaming now?

VK-Q6dowbzs.speaker_note: the community imam leading his annual pre-Ramadan fiqh session; mentions his wife fielding calls and his own rulings
VK-Q6dowbzs.title: The Fiqh of Fasting
VK-Q6dowbzs.one_line: Pre-Ramadan fiqh session: intention, what breaks and does not break the fast, disputed medical cases, valid excuses, make-up and expiation.
VK-Q6dowbzs.summary: Two weeks before Ramadan he says every act of worship needs outward fiqh and inner preparation, and this session covers the fiqh. Intention must precede the fast; he adopts Imam Malik's view that one intention covers the month, against the majority's nightly intention. His rule of thumb is that anything entering the body that nourishes breaks the fast. He lists six agreed invalidators, stressing that the first three break it only when deliberate, then six things that do not: brushing or siwak, eating forgetfully (and not interrupting someone who does), wet dreams, non-nutritive injections, swallowing saliva, and leftover wudu water, under the principle that what cannot be guarded against is excused. On four disputed modern cases he allows inhalers and, with conditions, eye and ear drops, but holds that intravenous fluids and enemas break the fast, while washing after the toilet does not. Illness, travel beyond about 80 km, pregnancy and nursing, and severe exhaustion are excuses, but labourers must still intend each day and break only when harm looms; for serious illness breaking becomes obligatory because bodily health precedes religious observance. He ends with make-up before the next Ramadan, urging women to spread make-up days through the year, and the major expiation for intercourse.

outline.heading: Every worship has an outward and an inner side
outline.gist: Without fiqh the act is invalid, without presence of heart it yields nothing; this session covers outward fiqh of Ramadan.

outline.heading: The companions prepared for Ramadan for months
outline.gist: They prayed six months to reach Ramadan and six months to have it accepted.

outline.heading: Intention as a precondition of the fast
outline.gist: Unlike prayer, the fast's intention must precede it; al-Shafi'i requires it every night, and waking for suhoor counts as intention.

outline.heading: Imam Malik: one intention for the whole month
outline.gist: The majority invalidate a fast begun without overnight intention; he adopts Malik's single intention at the start of Ramadan.

outline.heading: Verbalizing the intention
outline.gist: Saying it aloud after Isha, common in Shafi'i mosques, is fine but required for no intention except Hajj.

outline.heading: The general rule: nourishment entering the body
outline.gist: Anything entering the body that nourishes it breaks the fast by any route; classical texts predate injections and inhalers.

outline.heading: Six agreed invalidators
outline.gist: Deliberate eating and drinking, intercourse or emission, deliberate vomiting, intravenous feeding, smoking of any kind, and menstruation or postpartum bleeding.

outline.heading: Deliberate versus unintended
outline.gist: The first three break the fast only when deliberate; smoking, IV feeding and bleeding break it regardless; postpartum women may need to make up a whole month.

outline.heading: Brushing and siwak do not break the fast
outline.gist: Toothpaste and siwak are allowed all day, as al-Nawawi concluded.

outline.heading: Eating forgetfully, and not interrupting others
outline.gist: Fasting is between you and Allah; if you see someone eating forgetfully, let him finish before reminding him, except a smoker.

outline.heading: Unintended emission
outline.gist: A wet dream after fajr does not affect the fast.

outline.heading: Non-nutritive injections
outline.gist: Intramuscular and subcutaneous injections such as insulin, blood thinners or antibiotics do not break the fast; vitamins are best delayed.

outline.heading: Swallowing saliva
outline.gist: Even deliberately gathered saliva does not break the fast, though it is disliked.

outline.heading: Water left after wudu
outline.gist: Rinse normally without exaggeration; what remains after wudu does not break the fast.

outline.heading: What cannot be guarded against is excused
outline.gist: A fiqh principle: you are accountable only for negligence, not for traces no one can avoid.

outline.heading: Four disputed modern cases
outline.gist: He gives his view on each so worship is sound, without making listeners jurists.

outline.heading: Inhalers do not break the fast
outline.gist: Unlike smoke, an inhaler provides no nourishment and only opens the airways, so he permits it.

outline.heading: Eye and ear drops with conditions
outline.gist: Allowed when needed, non-nutritive, and if nothing reaches the throat; if it does, make up the day as a precaution.

outline.heading: Intravenous fluids break the fast
outline.gist: Even non-nutritive IV fluids fill the veins and reduce hunger and thirst; one needing them is ill and excused anyway.

outline.heading: Enemas break the fast
outline.gist: Most scholars hold that anything entering by either passage breaks it.

outline.heading: Washing after the toilet does not
outline.gist: Istinja with water is not absorbed and has no text against it, so do not avoid it while fasting.

outline.heading: His positions on the four cases
outline.gist: Inhalers and drops are permitted with conditions; IV and enemas break the fast.

outline.heading: Illness as an excuse, defined by medicine
outline.gist: Medicine is the authority on the body, as earlier jurists consulted the physicians of their day.

outline.heading: Ask your doctor
outline.gist: A non-Muslim doctor can judge whether fasting harms you; seek a Muslim doctor only if unsatisfied.

outline.heading: Health of the body comes before observance
outline.gist: When fasting endangers a chronically ill person, breaking it becomes obligatory, as with eating pork to avoid starvation.

outline.heading: Concession versus obligation to break
outline.gist: A mild infection allows breaking; kidney failure or advanced disease forbids fasting.

outline.heading: Travel: distance and length of stay
outline.gist: Breaking is allowed beyond about 80 km even in comfort; stays beyond several days or two weeks enter disagreement, so ask before long trips.

outline.heading: Pregnancy and nursing
outline.gist: Both are valid excuses, with expiation discussed later.

outline.heading: Severe exhaustion: intend each day, break only when needed
outline.gist: A roofer in a long Canadian summer fast must still intend and start each fast, breaking only when harm looms, with make-up and no expiation.

outline.heading: Your livelihood matters
outline.gist: Quitting work to fast would close your door of provision; work and make up the day in winter.

outline.heading: Making up missed days
outline.gist: The majority require make-up even for deliberate breaking; a minority say it cannot be made up, out of reverence for Ramadan.

outline.heading: Spread make-up days through the year
outline.gist: Delaying past the next Ramadan adds expiation; he urges women to fast one day a week rather than cramming before Ramadan.

outline.heading: The major expiation for intercourse

5tihQT0rvzo.speaker: adnan
5tihQT0rvzo.speaker_note: Continues his own Understanding Islam series and restates the points in Arabic in the second khutbah.
5tihQT0rvzo.title: Understanding Islam: The Outcomes (Part 1)
5tihQT0rvzo.one_line: The five worldly outcomes of practising Islam properly for the individual: fulfillment, harmony and direction, and integrity of ethics, thought and relationships.
5tihQT0rvzo.summary: The sheikh opens with the state of the world: the leader of the most powerful empire speaks without basic human decency, democracies cannot elect decent people, and Muslims in the West, unlike in the countries many fled, have a voice and must stop avoiding politics. That crisis is why he keeps returning to basics. Earlier generations had the leisure to argue details; a failing, uncentralized ummah does not, and Islam is highly functional in its simplest form. After recapping his model (Islam, Iman and Ihsan, held together by mortality and accountability), he argues that Allah did not offer a choice between enjoying this life and saving the next: following His way brings well-being in both. He then names five individual outcomes. Fulfillment fills the inner black hole that wealth, substances and milestones cannot, and leaves no one any leverage over you, as with the Prophet. Synchrony gives harmony with creation and a sense of direction, like facing the qiblah from anywhere. Then come incorruptible ethics that let you respect yourself, integrity of thought, and sound relationships beginning with Allah. Getting the recipe right requires learning from a chain of teachers, not Google or AI. He closes with a companion who kept reciting in prayer while struck by arrows.

outline.heading: The worst leadership in history
outline.gist: The leader of the largest empire on the planet speaks with no respect for other human beings, and with more people on the boat than ever, the suffering will be unparalleled. Democracies that cannot elect people with basic decency show a flaw in the process, and Muslims cannot leave this on the periphery.

outline.heading: We have a voice here
outline.gist: For two centuries Muslims have kept away from politics because they come from countries where you cannot even dream of it without waking in fear. In the West we can influence and have impact, so we must care.

outline.heading: When we had the luxury of details
outline.gist: Anyone engaged in a theology for long starts caring about the nitty-gritty and the controversies. There was a time Muslims could argue them ferociously and take pride in the intellectual output; today we do not have that luxury.

outline.heading: Back to the functional core
outline.gist: The ummah is failing, with no centralized politics, finances or spiritual leadership. Islam in its simplest form is highly functional, so go back to it, find what the companions found, and zoom out to see where your responsibility lies.

outline.heading: The model so far
outline.gist: Recap: Islam, Iman and Ihsan, held together by mortality and accountability, and the premise of the journey: a servant and steward who lives selflessly now to enjoy selfishness later, building a community that competes to do good.

outline.heading: Not misery here for Paradise later
outline.gist: Even if the choice were misery now and Paradise later, logic would still choose Paradise. But Allah did not frame it that way: live as He explains and you are well in this world and the next; refuse and you are miserable in both, so the choice is a no-brainer.

outline.heading: Outcomes here, for you and for the ummah
outline.gist: The outcomes in the hereafter are undisputed. He turns to the outcomes in this world for whoever learns their theology, fiqh and Ihsan and keeps mortality and accountability in view: five for the individual and three for the ummah.

outline.heading: Outcome 1: fulfillment
outline.gist: What people call happiness or joy is really a search for fulfillment. Comedians can make you laugh, but when they leave, are you calm and meaningful inside? Otherwise there is a black hole that devours everything and grows hungrier the more you feed it.

outline.heading: Not in a bottle, a pill or a physique
outline.gist: The young can distract themselves on the highway of life, but it slows down. Without fulfillment you end up middle-aged with spouse, children, degrees and money, asking why you are so sad.

outline.heading: No one can take it from you
outline.gist: Fulfillment lives inside you. They can take your wealth, health, country and status and it does not touch you, because its source is sacred and beyond their control, so no one has leverage on you.

outline.heading: Why live miserable between milestones?
outline.gist: Being miserable for two years to reach a milestone that gives a moment and a few photos is no way to live. Work toward goals, but be fulfilled every day; only Allah fills that hungry void.

outline.heading: No leverage on the Prophet
outline.gist: Fulfillment is liberating because no job or money can be held over you. The Quraysh leveraged the Prophet's uncle, family and home, and nothing worked, because what he had came from Allah.

outline.heading: Paradise before Paradise
outline.gist: The Prophet lived in satisfaction. The believer lives well, heart at ease and chest open, and finds a paradise in this life before being granted the next. If you lack fulfillment, ask what is missing.

outline.heading: Outcome 2: synchrony with creation
outline.gist: You feel at one with the world: the human race is a family you care for, and every living thing is your concern. The Prophet spoke to trees, rocks and the new crescent, telling it that his Lord and its Lord is Allah.

outline.heading: A sense of direction
outline.gist: Blindfold you, spin you and drop you anywhere, and you will find Makkah and pray; literally and figuratively you know where you are going and who you are. Even without the Kaaba we would face it, and tawaf turns counterclockwise like everything from the atom to the galaxies.

outline.heading: Outcome 3: incorruptible ethics and values
outline.gist: Integrity here means incorruptibility. Your values generate every action and reaction, so with strong, well-defined principles you make the right choice and do not cheat, lie, mistreat or backstab.

outline.heading: Respecting the person in the mirror
outline.gist: When you are older, wealth, status and applause mean nothing if you cannot respect yourself. Knowing you cheated your way to the money or the degrees on the wall, or wearing a mask, makes life impossible; Islam guards your ethics so you can respect yourself.

outline.heading: Outcome 4: integrity of thought
outline.gist: The world needs clear thinking free of bias, bigotry, ignorance and racism to solve problems that are catastrophic. The first word the ummah heard from the sky was about knowledge; what we prioritize and value has to change, and Allah teaches us how to learn.

outline.heading: Outcome 5: integrity of relationships, first with Allah
outline.gist: You know who Allah is, how to speak to Him and how to read the messages He sends. That relationship is so beautiful it can distract: the companions had to be told to leave the masjid and go serve the world.

outline.heading: Get the recipe right
outline.gist: This is achievable: the right amounts of Islam, Iman and Ihsan, the pan of mortality and the oven of the premise, and you get the cake. Without the recipe you cook garbage.

outline.heading: Not from Google, influencers or AI
outline.gist: Google, someone who wants to be followed, or AI cannot teach you the deen; wanting to be watched already shows you do not know the recipe. Unless you learn from someone who learned, in a chain back to Muhammad, you will get lost.

outline.heading: Focus on the basics
outline.gist: Even with a chain it is hard. Check your rituals, your beliefs and your Ihsan, keep mortality and accountability near, and walk with your eye on the prize; the outcome is fulfillment, direction and integrity.

outline.heading: Live well, not with wealth
outline.gist: Beyond enough to eat and a roof, money adds nothing: sociological studies show happiness plateaus around 60k a year. Living well comes from the recipe, so pick it up and start cooking.

outline.heading: Second khutbah in Arabic
outline.gist: He restates the five individual outcomes in Arabic.

outline.heading: How high is this on your priority list?
outline.gist: It will not be handed to you; it takes discipline and work, and it is beautiful when you reach it. That is how the companions lived.

outline.heading: Reciting through the arrows
outline.gist: A companion standing guard in prayer was struck by arrows and kept reciting until his blood woke his friend. He would rather die than cut his surah short: that is not philosophy but someone who found what we have yet to find.
